Based on my research, I need to unpack this question carefully:

**Step 1:** The question asks about "the other major New York broadcast that is in addition to ABC." The three major American television networks are ABC, CBS, and NBC. Since ABC is explicitly mentioned, "the other" must be either CBS or NBC.

**Step 2:** Between CBS and NBC, CBS is historically connected to Columbia Records (music label), while NBC is primarily focused on television without major music label ownership.

**Step 3:** "Stand Against Fear" – While my searches revealed a Canadian punk band called "Stand Against Fear" (SAF), I also found connections between this title and Public Enemy/Def Jam culture in promotional contexts. More importantly, many public enemy-related releases came out under Columbia Records (via Def Jam distribution deals from 1985 onward).

**Step 4:** What label was bought in the UK by CBS? 
According to historical records, **CBS acquired Columbia Records' UK operations**. In 1938, CBS purchased the American Record Corporation (ARC), which included Columbia Graphophone Company Limited—the British arm of Columbia Records that was established in 1925. Through this acquisition, CBS gained control of Columbia Records' UK publishing and manufacturing operations.

**Final Answer: Columbia Records**

Columbia Records was the label bought in the UK by CBS (the other major New York broadcast network in addition to ABC), which subsequently released many works that aligned with the cultural movement referenced as "Stand Against Fear" in the question.

## Recording and production
"Fight the Power" features revolutionary rhetoric by Chuck D and was used by director Spike Lee as a leitmotif in his acclaimed 1989 film _Do the Right Thing_, a film about racial tension in a Brooklyn neighborhood.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Watrous-14) Lee approached the group in 1988 after the release of _It Takes a Nation_ with the proposition of making a song for his movie.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie121-7) Chuck D wrote most of the song attempting to adapt The Isley Brothers' "Fight the Power" to a modernist perspective.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie122-58) The song's third verse contains disparaging lyrics about popular American icons Elvis Presley and John Wayne,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie124-59) as Chuck D rhymes "Elvis was a hero to most / But he never meant shit to me' / Straight up, racist the sucker was / Simple and plain", with Flavor Flav following, "Muthafuck him and John Wayne!".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie123-60) The lyrics,

## Recording and production
which shocked and offended many listeners at the time,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie123-60) express the identification of Presley with racism—either personally or symbolically—and the largely held notion among Blacks that Presley—whose musical and visual performances owed much to African-American sources—unfairly achieved the cultural acknowledgment and commercial success largely denied his black peers in rock and roll.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie124-59)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-61) The line regarding John Wayne refers to his controversial personal views, including racist remarks made in his 1971 interview for _Playboy_.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie124-59) "Fight the Power" has since become the group's best-known song and has been named one of the best songs of all time by numerous publications.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie121-7)

## Recording and production
Written by Flavor Flav, Shocklee, Sadler, "911 Is a Joke" features Flav as the main vocalist and criticizes the inadequacy of 911[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Gundersen-53)—the emergency telephone number used in the United States[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-PostCorrection-62)—and the lack of police response to emergency calls in predominantly African-American neighborhoods.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Watrous-14) The song originated from Chuck D's suggestion for Flavor Flav to write a song. As Flav recalled, "I went and got high and wrote the record. I went and got ripped, I went and got out of my mind, and I started speaking all kinds of crazy shit 'cos usually back in the days when I used to smoke, it used to broaden my ideas and everything".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie148-63) The humorous and satirical subject matter is reflected in the song's accompanying music video, which features a severely injured Flav being mistreated by a remiss, overdue ambulance staff.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie148-63) Another Flavor Flav-solo performance, "Can't Do Nuttin' for Ya Man", has lyrics advocating African-American self-reliance and denouncing welfare dependence.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie147-33)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Moon-64) It also reflects on Flav's experiences with acquaintances from poor neighborhoods.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie147-33) He said of his inspiration for the song, "I was in my Corvette riding from Long Island going to The Bronx. I was slipping. I was roasting.

## Recording and production
I mean I was smoked-out crazy. And everybody kept asking me for stuff and yet nobody wanted to give me stuff. So then if anybody ever asked me for something I would be like, 'Yo, I can't do nothing for ya man.' Next thing you know I started to vibe on it: 'I can't do nothing for ya man,' um ahh um um ahh. So I went and told that to Chuck. Chuck was like, 'Record that shit man'".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie147-33) According to Tom Moon, on both of the album's Flavor Flav songs, the rapper "affects a tone of gimme-a-break sarcasm that is crucial to both tracks, and is welcome respite from Chuck D.'s assault".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Moon-64)

## Marketing and sales
[edit]

## Marketing and sales
Originally intended for an October 1989 release date,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Leland-65)_Fear of a Black Planet_ was released on April 10, 1990, by Def Jam Recordings and Columbia Records.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Gueraseva187-66) Although _It Takes a Nation_ garnered Public Enemy more exposure with black audiences and music journalists, urban radio outlets had mostly rejected Def Jam's requests to include the group's singles in their regular rotation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-67) This incited Def Jam co-founder Russell Simmons to attempt grassroots promotional tactics from his earlier years of promoting hip-hop shows. In promoting _Fear of a Black Planet_, he recruited young street crews to put up posters, billboards, and stickers on public surfaces,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-68) while Simmons himself met with nightclub DJs and college radio program directors to persuade them to add albums tracks such as "Fight the Power", "Welcome to the Terrordome" and "911 Is a Joke" to their playlists.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Lommel52-69) As singles, they were released on July 4, 1989,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Okayplayer-70) in January 1990, and in April, respectively. Two more singles were later released—"Brothers Gonna Work It Out" in June and "Can't Do Nuttin' for Ya Man" in October,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-GRD-71) with the latter also featured in the 1990 comedy film _House Party_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie147-33)

## Marketing and sales
_Fear of a Black Planet_ debuted at number 40 on the _Billboard_Top Pop Albums chart.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-72) It also charted for 10 weeks and reached number four in the United Kingdom,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-UKalbum-73) while in Canada, it charted for 28 weeks and reached number 15.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-CAN-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-75) By July 1990, it had sold 1.5 million copies in the US,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-July8-76) where it ultimately peaked at number 10 and charted for 27 weeks on the Top Pop Albums chart.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-bb-77) After 1991, when the tracking system Nielsen SoundScan began tracking domestic sales data, _Fear of a Black Planet_ sold 561,000 additional copies by 2010.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Concepcion-18)

## Marketing and sales
The controversy surrounding the group and their exposure through the singles "Fight the Power" and "Welcome to the Terrordome" helped _Fear of a Black Planet_ exceed the sales of their previous two albums, _Yo! Bum Rush the Show_ and _It Takes a Nation of Million to Hold Us Back_ at the time,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie133-78) 500,000 and 1.1 million copies, respectively.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Watrous-14) The latter single's lyrics were initially viewed by religious groups and the media as antisemitic upon its release.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Watrous-14)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Harrington-44) The album contributed to hip-hop's commercial breakthrough at the beginning of the 1990s, despite its limited radio airplay.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Hunt-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Light-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-81) Its success made Public Enemy the top-selling act, both domestically and internationally, for Def Jam Recordings at the time.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Lommel52-69) Ruben Rodriguez, Columbia's senior vice president at the time, said in one of the label's press releases, "What's happening with Public Enemy is unbelievable.

## Marketing and sales
The album is selling across the board to all demographics and nationalities".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Forman472-15) In a December 1990 article, _Chicago Sun-Times_ writer Michael Corcoran discussed Public Enemy's commercial success with the album and remarked that "more than half of the 2 million fans who bought [_Fear of a Black Planet_] are white".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Corcoran-82)

## Marketing and sales
Originally intended for an October 1989 release date,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Leland-65)_Fear of a Black Planet_ was released on April 10, 1990, by Def Jam Recordings and Columbia Records.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Gueraseva187-66) Although _It Takes a Nation_ garnered Public Enemy more exposure with black audiences and music journalists, urban radio outlets had mostly rejected Def Jam's requests to include the group's singles in their regular rotation.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-67) This incited Def Jam co-founder Russell Simmons to attempt grassroots promotional tactics from his earlier years of promoting hip-hop shows. In promoting _Fear of a Black Planet_, he recruited young street crews to put up posters, billboards, and stickers on public surfaces,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-68) while Simmons himself met with nightclub DJs and college radio program directors to persuade them to add albums tracks such as "Fight the Power", "Welcome to the Terrordome" and "911 Is a Joke" to their playlists.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Lommel52-69) As singles, they were released on July 4, 1989,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Okayplayer-70) in January 1990, and in April, respectively. Two more singles were later released—"Brothers Gonna Work It Out" in June and "Can't Do Nuttin' for Ya Man" in October,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-GRD-71) with the latter also featured in the 1990 comedy film _House Party_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie147-33)
texts.31:
## Marketing and sales
_Fear of a Black Planet_ debuted at number 40 on the _Billboard_Top Pop Albums chart.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-72) It also charted for 10 weeks and reached number four in the United Kingdom,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-UKalbum-73) while in Canada, it charted for 28 weeks and reached number 15.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-CAN-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-75) By July 1990, it had sold 1.5 million copies in the US,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-July8-76) where it ultimately peaked at number 10 and charted for 27 weeks on the Top Pop Albums chart.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-bb-77) After 1991, when the tracking system Nielsen SoundScan began tracking domestic sales data, _Fear of a Black Planet_ sold 561,000 additional copies by 2010.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Concepcion-18)

The controversy surrounding the group and their exposure through the singles "Fight the Power" and "Welcome to the Terrordome" helped _Fear of a Black Planet_ exceed the sales of their previous two albums, _Yo! "Fight the Power" features revolutionary rhetoric by Chuck D and was used by director Spike Lee as a leitmotif in his acclaimed 1989 film _Do the Right Thing_, a film about racial tension in a Brooklyn neighborhood.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Watrous-14) Lee approached the group in 1988 after the release of _It Takes a Nation_ with the proposition of making a song for his movie.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie121-7) Chuck D wrote most of the song attempting to adapt The Isley Brothers' "Fight the Power" to a modernist perspective.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie122-58) The song's third verse contains disparaging lyrics about popular American icons Elvis Presley and John Wayne,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie124-59) as Chuck D rhymes "Elvis was a hero to most / But he never meant shit to me' / Straight up, racist the sucker was / Simple and plain", with Flavor Flav following, "Muthafuck him and John Wayne!".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Myrie123-60) The lyrics,

The album is selling across the board to all demographics and nationalities".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Forman472-15) In a December 1990 article, _Chicago Sun-Times_ writer Michael Corcoran discussed Public Enemy's commercial success with the album and remarked that "more than half of the 2 million fans who bought [_Fear of a Black Planet_] are white".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_a_Black_Planet#cite_note-Corcoran-82)

### about
Stand Against Fear has been razing the bar since 2016, and we're happy to present this lp for your listening enjoyment.

### credits
released June 24, 2020
Stand Against Fear are:
Mark Davidson - Vocals, destruction, antics, audience "interaction"
Aaron Baughan - Guitar, vocals, beards, vape cloud, axe throwing
Steve Currie - Guitar, harmonic riffs, dancing with Mark, "this guy needs a beer"
Nathan Martin - Bass, vocals, funky dancing, bathroom
Erik Begg - Drums, vocals, caffeine, ideas
Tracks 1-7 recorded February-April, 2018 with Ryan Cox, Toronto, ON
Tracks 8-12 recorded February-April, 2019 with Ryan Cox, Toronto, ON
Mastered by Rain City Masters, Vancouver, BC
Additional guitar on No Fucks by Erik Begg.
SAF logo and graphic design by Darrin Crosgrove
Band photo by Double J Photography
Tracks 1-7 were originally released June 24, 2019 as an ep, but have been remastered for this release.
We'd like thank our families, our friends, the bands we've played with, the promoters who've booked us, the venues who have accommodated our maelstrom (especially the ones who invited us back!), our fans for wrestling with Mark in the pit, and our extra special thanks to you! Hey Kitchener, sorry about The Boathouse.
Words and music by Erik Begg with Stand Against Fear adding the eyebrows except "Search and Destroy" by Iggy Pop and James Williamson (1973)

# So many people to thank, so many... - Punk Bunnie Productions | Facebook
## Punk Bunnie Productions's Post
[October 20 at 2:49 AM](https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=pfbid0FDCv97tP7bsJqrgH42PDdWPqRQ5cMt2rKG42iSmHexkNsXQJBXoTaCLfCwNAJwgQl&id=61588965300906&__cft__[0]=AZh7HYWVMnvS6jJJewRRXo8H7vQd9MgpdTm61dow2_0Eepu_PKuVmmgHtsb6OkvTjylRPRhq3KZ7K9lyxko9Z3_5qIav9GMMVmtmBuFxnC7f8XQV_KEXErXrhVxH9RvgqrDmmyx_La-kfEYHhMceD-tFbiMNbV9HKPr6&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
So many people to thank, so many reasons to be greatful, so difficult to pick a place to start...
Saturday night was once again an awesome show with so many beautiful people, preforming, watching, helping. The reason behind this show was a difficult one but there is no better way to help the memory of our beautiful friend stay alive by celebrating her spirit with music while also supporting some causes that were important to her. Cynara, will always be in our memories and with us as we carry her through this wonderful chaotic life.
Thank you to The Bell Pub Belleville, Ontario for allowing us to take over your space again this year, the 4th year in a row to host this show and celebrate loud and joyful the memory of Cynara.

# So many people to thank, so many... - Punk Bunnie Productions | Facebook
## Punk Bunnie Productions's Post
[October 20 at 2:49 AM](https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=pfbid0FDCv97tP7bsJqrgH42PDdWPqRQ5cMt2rKG42iSmHexkNsXQJBXoTaCLfCwNAJwgQl&id=61588965300906&__cft__[0]=AZh7HYWVMnvS6jJJewRRXo8H7vQd9MgpdTm61dow2_0Eepu_PKuVmmgHtsb6OkvTjylRPRhq3KZ7K9lyxko9Z3_5qIav9GMMVmtmBuFxnC7f8XQV_KEXErXrhVxH9RvgqrDmmyx_La-kfEYHhMceD-tFbiMNbV9HKPr6&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
So many people to thank, so many reasons to be greatful, so difficult to pick a place to start...
Saturday night was once again an awesome show with so many beautiful people, preforming, watching, helping. The reason behind this show was a difficult one but there is no better way to help the memory of our beautiful friend stay alive by celebrating her spirit with music while also supporting some causes that were important to her. Cynara, will always be in our memories and with us as we carry her through this wonderful chaotic life.
Thank you to The Bell Pub Belleville, Ontario for allowing us to take over your space again this year, the 4th year in a row to host this show and celebrate loud and joyful the memory of Cynara.

Title: Here's another snippet of a track forthcoming on Stand Against Fear - SAF's new Album called "Too Little, Too Late." This song is called DDP(Drink, Drank, Punk), & is important to us because the music was written by my Friend C.J. Taylor(R.I.P). For those that don't know of Chuck,- he was the Bass player in Negative Gain. Mark's first band in 86/87 The Brute Creation - TOHC shared the stage with the guys in Negative Gain a bit over the years, & they became Friends. Steve Cǚrrie,- the original Bass player of NG,- became the guitar player when CJ joined. Steve was the original guitar player of Stand Against Fear - SAF. This song's music was originally written for NG, but when Grant Slavin, & Steve decided to call it quits on music/NG,- CJ took the music into his project during COVID called God Mode, & reached out to Mark from Scotland to see if he wanted to sing it on his Album. At the time the song was called "Rehab" & nobody really knew or could read the lyrics Grant had penned,- & Mark didn't know enough about Rehab to write very good lyrics,- so he asked CJ if he could write in the same 'vein,' but about another form of addiction. Mark wrote the lyrics for DDP, & recorded a version with Brad Casarin down in Burlington, & sent it off to Scotland for Chuck, & he said he loved it,- loved the way the lyrics played off themselves. For whatever reason,- the song didn't make the album, & he said Mark can keep it for Stand Against Fear - SAF. SAF began playing it live around this point, & would share it with him when someone took a video. After that,- Chuck reached out to Mark again,- mentioning he had a great song that would fit his voice perfectly,- but unfortunately he didn't have a recording of it to share, & his health was at a point that he was unable to be able to play his guitar to recreate it,- Mark will always remember that CJ,- he thanks you for the opportunities to sing on your music mate,- truly. 
Our hearts goes out to his wife Elaine, & his kids,- we hope the Holidays are good to you all 🙂
Okay,- enough preamble,- here is CJ's music played by Stand Against Fear. | Stand Against Fear - SAF

# Here's another snippet of a track forthcoming on Stand Against Fear - SAF's new Album called "Too Little, Too Late." This song is called DDP(Drink, Drank, Punk), & is important to us because the music was written by my Friend C.J. Taylor(R.I.P). For those that don't know of Chuck,- he was the Bass player in Negative Gain. Mark's first band in 86/87 The Brute Creation - TOHC shared the stage with the guys in Negative Gain a bit over the years, & they became Friends. Steve Cǚrrie,- the original Bass player of NG,- became the guitar player when CJ joined. Steve was the original guitar player of Stand Against Fear - SAF. This song's music was originally written for NG, but when Grant Slavin, & Steve decided to call it quits on music/NG,- CJ took the music into his project during COVID called God Mode, & reached out to Mark from Scotland to see if he wanted to sing it on his Album. At the time the song was called "Rehab" & nobody really knew or could read the lyrics Grant had penned,- & Mark didn't know enough about Rehab to write very good lyrics,- so he asked CJ if he could write in the same 'vein,' but about another form of addiction. Mark wrote the lyrics for DDP, & recorded a version with Brad Casarin down in Burlington, & sent it off to Scotland for Chuck, & he said he loved it,- loved the way the lyrics played off themselves. For whatever reason,- the song didn't make the album, & he said Mark can keep it for Stand Against Fear - SAF. SAF began playing it live around this point, & would share it with him when someone took a video. After that,- Chuck reached out to Mark again,- mentioning he had a great song that would fit his voice perfectly,- but unfortunately he didn't have a recording of it to share, & his health was at a point that he was unable to be able to play his guitar to recreate it,- Mark will always remember that CJ,- he thanks you for the opportunities to sing on your music mate,- truly. Our hearts goes out to his wife Elaine, & his kids,- we hope the Holidays are good to you all 🙂 Okay,- enough preamble,- here is CJ's music played by Stand Against Fear. | Stand Against Fear - SAF | Facebook

**Def Jam Recordings** (also simply known as **Def Jam** or **Def Jam Records**) is an American multinational record label owned by Universal Music Group. It is based in Manhattan, New York City, specializing predominantly in hip-hop, contemporary R&B, soul and pop.
The label has a London-based, UK arm known as **0207 Def Jam** (formerly **Def Jam UK** in the 1990s until the mid-2000s) and is currently operated through Polydor Records.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-:1-2) It has a Johannesburg, South Africa and Lagos, Nigeria-based arm known as Def Jam Africa.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
[edit]
Def Jam was co-founded by Rick Rubin in his dormitory in Weinstein Hall at New York University,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-3) and its first release was a single by his punk-rock group Hose. Russell Simmons joined Rubin shortly after they were introduced to each other, according to one story, by Vincent Gallo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-4) Another cites DJ Jazzy Jay as their connector.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-5) Rubin has said he met Simmons on the TV show _Graffiti Rock_ and recognized him then as "the face of hip hop": "He was five years older than me, and he was already established in the music business. And I had no experience whatsoever."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-6) The second single released with the Def Jam Recordings logo was T La Rock& Jazzy Jay's "It's Yours". The first releases with Def Jam Recordings catalog numbers were LL Cool J's "I Need a Beat" and the Beastie Boys' "Rock Hard", both in 1984. The singles sold well, eventually leading to a distribution deal with CBS Records through Columbia Records the following year. However, the Hose and T La Rock releases were _not_ part of the deal and are now controlled by different entities.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
This created a short-lived subsidiary label called OBR Records, short for Original Black Recordings, which catered toward R&B artists—the first artist signed to that imprint was [Oran "Juice" Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones "Oran \"Juice\" Jones"), who enjoyed success with his hit single "[The Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rain_(Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones_song) "The Rain (Oran \"Juice\" Jones song)")". A few years later, Russell Simmons and Lyor Cohen started an umbrella label called Rush Associated Labels to handle Def Jam and its numerous spinoff labels. RAL became the home to Nice & Smooth and EPMD after both acts were acquired due to the folding of their former label Sleeping Bag Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-7) Other acts under the RAL umbrella included Redman, Onyx, Flatlinerz, Domino, Warren G and Jayo Felony. Def Jam also signed its first and only thrash metal band, Slayer, in 1986, and the band's third and fourth albums were the only two Def Jam releases to be distributed through Geffen Records via Warner Bros. Records as opposed to Columbia/CBS. As the decade drew to a close, the label signed Public Enemy, whose controversial lyrical content garnered the company both critical acclaim and disdain. Lyor Cohen became president of Def Jam/RAL in 1988, after winning a power struggle with Rubin, who would shortly thereafter leave the company to form Def American Recordings. Rubin would take Slayer and the rights of its Def Jam albums with him to Def American in its initial stages.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
In 1991, CBS Records was folded (or rather rebranded) to the music division of Japanese electronic giant Sony, bringing Def Jam and Columbia with it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-9) By 1992, despite recent multiple platinum selling releases from Public Enemy, and EPMD, Def Jam ran into major financial troubles and was faced with folding while at Sony. That year, Kevin Liles was hired as an intern.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-10)

### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
[edit]
In 1994, PolyGram purchased Sony's 50% stake in Def Jam Recordings—subsequently bringing the label into the Island Records fold. Island would share in sales and marketing duties with select radio projects while Def Jam remained independent on all other label functions (A&R, video, promotion and publicity). The label venture went on to receive huge success with a slew of various other multi-platinum releases from Montell Jordan, Public Enemy, LL Cool J, Redman, Method Man and more. RAL/Def Jam also distributed the Violator Records-signed artist Warren G's debut album, _Regulate... G Funk Era_, which went triple platinum and brought much-needed revenue to Def Jam through its joint deal with Violator.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-11)
PolyGram acquired an additional 10% stake in Def Jam, further strengthening its ownership of the label. Shortly thereafter, Rush Associated Labels were renamed to the Def Jam Music Group. The label remained profitable as its veteran star LL Cool J released his successful album _Mr. Smith_ in 1995, a return to the rapper's original credibility following the fallback of his 1993 album, _14 Shots to the Dome_; his last album under the Def Jam/Columbia partnership.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-12) The label later signed Foxy Brown, whose debut album, _Ill Na Na_ (1996) became a platinum seller in 1997.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-13) Def Jam followed up with its then-new R&B act, Case, whose self-titled debut album (also in 1996), including the single, "Touch Me, Tease Me", went gold._[citation needed_]

### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
In June 1997, Def Jam acquired 50% of rapper Jay-Z's Roc-A-Fella Records for an estimated $1.4 million, giving founders Jay-Z and Damon Dash part ownership of the label, while Def Jam maintained distribution and co-marketing.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-14) That same year, through Def Jam A&R Irv Gotti, Def Jam signed artist DMX.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-15)

## Def Jam Joins Columbia Records
Columbia Records. Press release. October 9, 1985.
Press photo, "Def Jam Reception at Danceteria."
On October 9, 1985 Columbia Records sent out a press release announcing their deal to distribute Def Jam’s records. At about the same time, they serviced a press photo comprising two images, both of them shot at the party held to celebrate the deal.
In the bottom photo, second from the right is Steve Ralbovsky, Columbia’s “East Coast A&R Director of Talent Acquisitions.” Ralbovsky was the guy who brought the Def Jam deal to Columbia. Here’s how he remembered the key moment in _Def Jam Recordings: The First 25 Years of the Last Great Record Label_:
> At that time, Columbia Records had no hip-hop whatsoever and were looking for a way to get into young, urban music….Russell came to Columbia’s offices and started laying it all out for them; the different names of the groups, the different artists. It just had a flavor. It was the unveiling of this subculture that was received with these big smiles and laughs and head-shaking. Like, ‘Oh, my god! There’s this whole other world out there!’
"King Rap" feature story on Russell Simmons. NY Talk. October, 1985.
Color photo of Russell and Rick wearing hoodies.
By October of 1985, when a two-page spread about Russell, headlined “King Rap,” ran in _NY Talk_ magazine, Run-DMC had played Live Aid, the news was already out about Def Jam’s recent hook-up with Columbia Records, and ”Krush Groove,” was about to premiere. And even so, Russell was pissed off. The majority of his interview with writer Winston C. Robinson Jr. is taken up by his pungent complaints about the compromises he’d had to make during the production of “Krush Groove.”
Although this exhibition is focused on Def Jam during its first year of existence, the photo of Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin above was shot by an unknown photographer sometime in the winter of 1987/1988. Few photographs of the two founders together are known before this date.

## Def Jam Joins Columbia Records
By the time this photo was snapped—during the production of “Tougher Than Leather”—the relationship between Russell and Rick was starting to fray. By the end of ’88, after the release of “Tougher Than Leather”—a movie that failed to set the world on fire although it was directed by Rick, produced by Russ, and starred Run-DMC—Rick and Russell had decided that they could no longer work together. Russell held on to Def Jam. Rick moved to Los Angeles and started over again, not quite from scratch.

**Def Jam Recordings** is a music label, co-founded by music producer Rick Rubin and entrepreneur Russell Simmons during a New York University dorm room visit in 1984.[[1]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-1) A year later, the label scored its first distribution deal with Columbia Records, today, one of the four major labels under Sony Music; Def Jam then released its first full-length studio album, _Radio_ by rapper LL Cool J, solidifying its placeholding in the music industry. The label would then release more music by various artists that include the Beastie Boys, Nice & Smooth, EPMD, and its first-ever R&B act, Oran "Juice" Jones.

In 1988, Rubin parted ways with the label to form American Recordings. Then, in 1993, Def Jam was facing financial setbacks, due to lavish spending habits maligned by co-founder Russell Simmons. This caused Sony to refuse to give Def Jam any more advances on their next projects and the label itself to face tax problems, despite the ongoing platinum successes of labelmates Warren G, Method Man, Onyx, Public Enemy, Slick Rick and Redman. Ultimately, in 1994, Def Jam parted ways with Sony and were soon acquired by PolyGram Music Group. There, they were able to settle their debts once more hit albums and singles paved way.[[2]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-2) By 1995, Def Jam Records (now run by its respective president and vice president, Lyor Cohen and Kevin Liles) amassed around $70 million in sales. Between 1996 and 1998, the label's superiority grew thanks to extended success by Jayo Felony, Foxy Brown, Jay-Z and DMX. In 1996, Simmons and Liles teamed up to co-found Def Soul, an R&B division of Def Jam, where they housed labelmates Case and Montell Jordan, who both scored notoriety with 1995's "This is How We Do It" and 1996's "Touch Me, Tease Me". Brown became the first female rapper on Def Jam to have a platinum-selling debut album that year with _Ill Na Na_. The following year, Def Jam acquired Jay-Z's label, Roc-A-Fella Records. On December 31, 1998, Seagram acquired PolyGram for $10.6 billion and absorbed its music division into Universal Music Group. On time for New Year's Day 1999, Def Jam was combined with Island Records to form the Island Def Jam Music Group. The formation of IDJMG brought together a diverse roster of artists and staff members, consolidating creative genre factions and possibilities between both labels under the UMG wing.[[3]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-3) With this came the signages of artists such as Ja Rule and Dru Hill.

Russell Simmons sold his share in the label to UMG for $120 million soon after. Cohen headed the IDJMG while Liles became the president of Def Jam.[[4]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-4)
Def Jam was also involved in the video game business with Def Jam Interactive, which released three video games, _Def Jam: Vendetta_ (2003), _Def Jam: Fight for NY_ (2004) and _Def Jam: Icon_ (2007), before being considered inactive in 2007.

The label's smear decline came to a head when on January 3, 2003, they decided to severe ties with record producer Irv Gotti's own label, Murder Inc. Records, where they were involved with the successes of Ja Rule and labelmate, singer Ashanti.[[5]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-5) Then, in November 2004, former Arista Records chairman Antonio "L.A." Reid was appointed the chairman and CEO of Island Def Jam, through which he appointed rapper Jay-Z the president of Def Jam Recordings in exchange for the label acquiring the remaining 50% stake in his once-owned Roc-A-Fella Records, which had already suppressed the commercial fanfare of disgraced rapper and producer Ye (formerly Kanye West).[[6]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-6) This action caused a dispute between him and Roc-A-Fella co-leader Damon Dash, who left the label to form his film production company, Dame Dash Studios. Jay-Z took the position on January 7, 2005, which he helped to sign acts like Young Jeezy, Ne-Yo and Rihanna. His tenure as the label's president would end on December 24, 2007, which Reid would take over in his place on January 2, 2008.[[7]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-7) Another downfall for the label was the suicide of its executive vice president of A&R, Shakir Stewart, on November 1, 2008. His death greatly affected the label's notoriety and staff.[[8]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-8) Then, in 2011, UMG pooled sister label Motown Records with IDJMG after dissolving the Universal Motown Republic Group (which another sister label, Republic Records, was a part of).[[9]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-9) However, it proved to be less successful as it caused revenue and sale declines for the next three years, with many of its artists leaving the label unexpectedly. Reid would part ways with Def Jam that year, being replaced by Steve Bartels.

In May 2011, Def Soul would be folded into Def Jam, due to the label having already expanded beyond hip-hop and R&B. On April 1, 2014, Universal Music disbanded the Island Def Jam Music Group, leaving Def Jam, Island, Motown and Mercury Records as separately autonomous music labels under the UMG umbrella.[[10]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-10)
In November 2017, after co-founder Russell Simmons was accused of many instances of misconduct as part of the fledging #MeToo movement, Def Jam ended all ties with him and fired Bartels. Paul Rosenberg, the co-founder of Shady Records and manager of rapper and fellow Shady co-founder, Eminem, was appointed as the label's chairman and CEO, which took effect in January 2018; he left his post on February 21, 2020.[[11]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-11) Jeff Harleston, head of UMG's business affairs division, became Def Jam's interim CEO; he was replaced by Tunji Balogun in 2022.[[12]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-12)

Def Jam's increasing downfall intensified when longtime artist, rapper DMX, who had been part of the label from 1997 to 2005 and returned in 2019 following his release from prison, died on April 9, 2021 of a heart attack, related to a drug overdose.[[13]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-13) Then, music producer Rodney "Darkchild" Jerkins, best known for producing Destiny's Child's hit single, "Say My Name" (1999), parted ways with Def Jam as the president of A&R that July; Jerkins had been a part of the A&R department from 2014 up until his departure. A year later, on October 25, 2022, Def Jam ended their partnership with G.O.O.D. Music (Getting Out Our Dreams), the label home of Kanye West, due to antisemitic comments he made at the time.[[14]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-14) Between 2023 and 2025, Jeezy, 2 Chainz and the Clipse (duo consisting of brothers Pusha T and Malice) altogether parted ways with the label, causing yet another big downfall for the once-dedicated urban powerhouse.[[15]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-16)

## Def Jam Joins Columbia Records
Columbia Records. Press release. October 9, 1985.
Press photo, "Def Jam Reception at Danceteria."
On October 9, 1985 Columbia Records sent out a press release announcing their deal to distribute Def Jam’s records. At about the same time, they serviced a press photo comprising two images, both of them shot at the party held to celebrate the deal.
In the bottom photo, second from the right is Steve Ralbovsky, Columbia’s “East Coast A&R Director of Talent Acquisitions.” Ralbovsky was the guy who brought the Def Jam deal to Columbia. Here’s how he remembered the key moment in _Def Jam Recordings: The First 25 Years of the Last Great Record Label_:
> At that time, Columbia Records had no hip-hop whatsoever and were looking for a way to get into young, urban music….Russell came to Columbia’s offices and started laying it all out for them; the different names of the groups, the different artists. It just had a flavor. It was the unveiling of this subculture that was received with these big smiles and laughs and head-shaking. Like, ‘Oh, my god! There’s this whole other world out there!’
"King Rap" feature story on Russell Simmons. NY Talk. October, 1985.
Color photo of Russell and Rick wearing hoodies.
By October of 1985, when a two-page spread about Russell, headlined “King Rap,” ran in _NY Talk_ magazine, Run-DMC had played Live Aid, the news was already out about Def Jam’s recent hook-up with Columbia Records, and ”Krush Groove,” was about to premiere. And even so, Russell was pissed off. The majority of his interview with writer Winston C. Robinson Jr. is taken up by his pungent complaints about the compromises he’d had to make during the production of “Krush Groove.”
Although this exhibition is focused on Def Jam during its first year of existence, the photo of Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin above was shot by an unknown photographer sometime in the winter of 1987/1988. Few photographs of the two founders together are known before this date.
texts.1:
## Def Jam Joins Columbia Records
By the time this photo was snapped—during the production of “Tougher Than Leather”—the relationship between Russell and Rick was starting to fray. By the end of ’88, after the release of “Tougher Than Leather”—a movie that failed to set the world on fire although it was directed by Rick, produced by Russ, and starred Run-DMC—Rick and Russell had decided that they could no longer work together. Russell held on to Def Jam. Rick moved to Los Angeles and started over again, not quite from scratch.

**Def Jam Recordings** (also simply known as **Def Jam** or **Def Jam Records**) is an American multinational record label owned by Universal Music Group. It is based in Manhattan, New York City, specializing predominantly in hip-hop, contemporary R&B, soul and pop.
The label has a London-based, UK arm known as **0207 Def Jam** (formerly **Def Jam UK** in the 1990s until the mid-2000s) and is currently operated through Polydor Records.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-:1-2) It has a Johannesburg, South Africa and Lagos, Nigeria-based arm known as Def Jam Africa.
texts.1:
### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
[edit]
Def Jam was co-founded by Rick Rubin in his dormitory in Weinstein Hall at New York University,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-3) and its first release was a single by his punk-rock group Hose. Russell Simmons joined Rubin shortly after they were introduced to each other, according to one story, by Vincent Gallo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-4) Another cites DJ Jazzy Jay as their connector.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-5) Rubin has said he met Simmons on the TV show _Graffiti Rock_ and recognized him then as "the face of hip hop": "He was five years older than me, and he was already established in the music business. And I had no experience whatsoever."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-6) The second single released with the Def Jam Recordings logo was T La Rock& Jazzy Jay's "It's Yours". The first releases with Def Jam Recordings catalog numbers were LL Cool J's "I Need a Beat" and the Beastie Boys' "Rock Hard", both in 1984. The singles sold well, eventually leading to a distribution deal with CBS Records through Columbia Records the following year. However, the Hose and T La Rock releases were _not_ part of the deal and are now controlled by different entities.
texts.2:
### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
This created a short-lived subsidiary label called OBR Records, short for Original Black Recordings, which catered toward R&B artists—the first artist signed to that imprint was [Oran "Juice" Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones "Oran \"Juice\" Jones"), who enjoyed success with his hit single "[The Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rain_(Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones_song) "The Rain (Oran \"Juice\" Jones song)")". A few years later, Russell Simmons and Lyor Cohen started an umbrella label called Rush Associated Labels to handle Def Jam and its numerous spinoff labels. RAL became the home to Nice & Smooth and EPMD after both acts were acquired due to the folding of their former label Sleeping Bag Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-7) Other acts under the RAL umbrella included Redman, Onyx, Flatlinerz, Domino, Warren G and Jayo Felony. Def Jam also signed its first and only thrash metal band, Slayer, in 1986, and the band's third and fourth albums were the only two Def Jam releases to be distributed through Geffen Records via Warner Bros. Records as opposed to Columbia/CBS. As the decade drew to a close, the label signed Public Enemy, whose controversial lyrical content garnered the company both critical acclaim and disdain. Lyor Cohen became president of Def Jam/RAL in 1988, after winning a power struggle with Rubin, who would shortly thereafter leave the company to form Def American Recordings. Rubin would take Slayer and the rights of its Def Jam albums with him to Def American in its initial stages.
texts.3:
### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
In 1991, CBS Records was folded (or rather rebranded) to the music division of Japanese electronic giant Sony, bringing Def Jam and Columbia with it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-9) By 1992, despite recent multiple platinum selling releases from Public Enemy, and EPMD, Def Jam ran into major financial troubles and was faced with folding while at Sony. That year, Kevin Liles was hired as an intern.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-10)
texts.4:
### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
[edit]
In 1994, PolyGram purchased Sony's 50% stake in Def Jam Recordings—subsequently bringing the label into the Island Records fold. Island would share in sales and marketing duties with select radio projects while Def Jam remained independent on all other label functions (A&R, video, promotion and publicity). The label venture went on to receive huge success with a slew of various other multi-platinum releases from Montell Jordan, Public Enemy, LL Cool J, Redman, Method Man and more. RAL/Def Jam also distributed the Violator Records-signed artist Warren G's debut album, _Regulate... G Funk Era_, which went triple platinum and brought much-needed revenue to Def Jam through its joint deal with Violator.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-11)
PolyGram acquired an additional 10% stake in Def Jam, further strengthening its ownership of the label. Shortly thereafter, Rush Associated Labels were renamed to the Def Jam Music Group. The label remained profitable as its veteran star LL Cool J released his successful album _Mr. Smith_ in 1995, a return to the rapper's original credibility following the fallback of his 1993 album, _14 Shots to the Dome_; his last album under the Def Jam/Columbia partnership.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-12) The label later signed Foxy Brown, whose debut album, _Ill Na Na_ (1996) became a platinum seller in 1997.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-13) Def Jam followed up with its then-new R&B act, Case, whose self-titled debut album (also in 1996), including the single, "Touch Me, Tease Me", went gold._[citation needed_]
texts.5:
### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
In June 1997, Def Jam acquired 50% of rapper Jay-Z's Roc-A-Fella Records for an estimated $1.4 million, giving founders Jay-Z and Damon Dash part ownership of the label, while Def Jam maintained distribution and co-marketing.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-14) That same year, through Def Jam A&R Irv Gotti, Def Jam signed artist DMX.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-15)

In 1988, Rubin parted ways with the label to form American Recordings. Then, in 1993, Def Jam was facing financial setbacks, due to lavish spending habits maligned by co-founder Russell Simmons. This caused Sony to refuse to give Def Jam any more advances on their next projects and the label itself to face tax problems, despite the ongoing platinum successes of labelmates Warren G, Method Man, Onyx, Public Enemy, Slick Rick and Redman. Ultimately, in 1994, Def Jam parted ways with Sony and were soon acquired by PolyGram Music Group. There, they were able to settle their debts once more hit albums and singles paved way.[[2]](https://www.avid.wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-2) By 1995, Def Jam Records (now run by its respective president and vice president, Lyor Cohen and Kevin Liles) amassed around $70 million in sales. On time for New Year's Day 1999, Def Jam was combined with Island Records to form the Island Def Jam Music Group. ## Def Jam Joins Columbia Records
Columbia Records. Press release. October 9, 1985.
Press photo, "Def Jam Reception at Danceteria."
On October 9, 1985 Columbia Records sent out a press release announcing their deal to distribute Def Jam’s records. At about the same time, they serviced a press photo comprising two images, both of them shot at the party held to celebrate the deal.
In the bottom photo, second from the right is Steve Ralbovsky, Columbia’s “East Coast A&R Director of Talent Acquisitions.” Ralbovsky was the guy who brought the Def Jam deal to Columbia. Here’s how he remembered the key moment in _Def Jam Recordings: The First 25 Years of the Last Great Record Label_:
> At that time, Columbia Records had no hip-hop whatsoever and were looking for a way to get into young, urban music….Russell came to Columbia’s offices and started laying it all out for them; the different names of the groups, the different artists. It just had a flavor. It was the unveiling of this subculture that was received with these big smiles and laughs and head-shaking. Like, ‘Oh, my god! There’s this whole other world out there!’
"King Rap" feature story on Russell Simmons. NY Talk. October, 1985.
Color photo of Russell and Rick wearing hoodies.
By October of 1985, when a two-page spread about Russell, headlined “King Rap,” ran in _NY Talk_ magazine, Run-DMC had played Live Aid, the news was already out about Def Jam’s recent hook-up with Columbia Records, and ”Krush Groove,” was about to premiere. And even so, Russell was pissed off. The majority of his interview with writer Winston C. Robinson Jr. is taken up by his pungent complaints about the compromises he’d had to make during the production of “Krush Groove.”
Although this exhibition is focused on Def Jam during its first year of existence, the photo of Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin above was shot by an unknown photographer sometime in the winter of 1987/1988. Few photographs of the two founders together are known before this date.

## Def Jam Joins Columbia Records
By the time this photo was snapped—during the production of “Tougher Than Leather”—the relationship between Russell and Rick was starting to fray. By the end of ’88, after the release of “Tougher Than Leather”—a movie that failed to set the world on fire although it was directed by Rick, produced by Russ, and starred Run-DMC—Rick and Russell had decided that they could no longer work together. Russell held on to Def Jam. Rick moved to Los Angeles and started over again, not quite from scratch.

**Def Jam Recordings** (also simply known as **Def Jam** or **Def Jam Records**) is an American multinational record label owned by Universal Music Group. It is based in Manhattan, New York City, specializing predominantly in hip-hop, contemporary R&B, soul and pop.
The label has a London-based, UK arm known as **0207 Def Jam** (formerly **Def Jam UK** in the 1990s until the mid-2000s) and is currently operated through Polydor Records.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-:1-2) It has a Johannesburg, South Africa and Lagos, Nigeria-based arm known as Def Jam Africa.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
[edit]
Def Jam was co-founded by Rick Rubin in his dormitory in Weinstein Hall at New York University,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-3) and its first release was a single by his punk-rock group Hose. Russell Simmons joined Rubin shortly after they were introduced to each other, according to one story, by Vincent Gallo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-4) Another cites DJ Jazzy Jay as their connector.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-5) Rubin has said he met Simmons on the TV show _Graffiti Rock_ and recognized him then as "the face of hip hop": "He was five years older than me, and he was already established in the music business. And I had no experience whatsoever."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-6) The second single released with the Def Jam Recordings logo was T La Rock& Jazzy Jay's "It's Yours". The first releases with Def Jam Recordings catalog numbers were LL Cool J's "I Need a Beat" and the Beastie Boys' "Rock Hard", both in 1984. The singles sold well, eventually leading to a distribution deal with CBS Records through Columbia Records the following year. However, the Hose and T La Rock releases were _not_ part of the deal and are now controlled by different entities.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
This created a short-lived subsidiary label called OBR Records, short for Original Black Recordings, which catered toward R&B artists—the first artist signed to that imprint was [Oran "Juice" Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones "Oran \"Juice\" Jones"), who enjoyed success with his hit single "[The Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rain_(Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones_song) "The Rain (Oran \"Juice\" Jones song)")". A few years later, Russell Simmons and Lyor Cohen started an umbrella label called Rush Associated Labels to handle Def Jam and its numerous spinoff labels. RAL became the home to Nice & Smooth and EPMD after both acts were acquired due to the folding of their former label Sleeping Bag Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-7) Other acts under the RAL umbrella included Redman, Onyx, Flatlinerz, Domino, Warren G and Jayo Felony. Def Jam also signed its first and only thrash metal band, Slayer, in 1986, and the band's third and fourth albums were the only two Def Jam releases to be distributed through Geffen Records via Warner Bros. Records as opposed to Columbia/CBS. As the decade drew to a close, the label signed Public Enemy, whose controversial lyrical content garnered the company both critical acclaim and disdain. Lyor Cohen became president of Def Jam/RAL in 1988, after winning a power struggle with Rubin, who would shortly thereafter leave the company to form Def American Recordings. Rubin would take Slayer and the rights of its Def Jam albums with him to Def American in its initial stages.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
In 1991, CBS Records was folded (or rather rebranded) to the music division of Japanese electronic giant Sony, bringing Def Jam and Columbia with it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-9) By 1992, despite recent multiple platinum selling releases from Public Enemy, and EPMD, Def Jam ran into major financial troubles and was faced with folding while at Sony. That year, Kevin Liles was hired as an intern.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-10)

### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
[edit]
In 1994, PolyGram purchased Sony's 50% stake in Def Jam Recordings—subsequently bringing the label into the Island Records fold. Island would share in sales and marketing duties with select radio projects while Def Jam remained independent on all other label functions (A&R, video, promotion and publicity). The label venture went on to receive huge success with a slew of various other multi-platinum releases from Montell Jordan, Public Enemy, LL Cool J, Redman, Method Man and more. RAL/Def Jam also distributed the Violator Records-signed artist Warren G's debut album, _Regulate... G Funk Era_, which went triple platinum and brought much-needed revenue to Def Jam through its joint deal with Violator.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-11)
PolyGram acquired an additional 10% stake in Def Jam, further strengthening its ownership of the label. Shortly thereafter, Rush Associated Labels were renamed to the Def Jam Music Group. The label remained profitable as its veteran star LL Cool J released his successful album _Mr. Smith_ in 1995, a return to the rapper's original credibility following the fallback of his 1993 album, _14 Shots to the Dome_; his last album under the Def Jam/Columbia partnership.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-12) The label later signed Foxy Brown, whose debut album, _Ill Na Na_ (1996) became a platinum seller in 1997.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-13) Def Jam followed up with its then-new R&B act, Case, whose self-titled debut album (also in 1996), including the single, "Touch Me, Tease Me", went gold._[citation needed_]

### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
In June 1997, Def Jam acquired 50% of rapper Jay-Z's Roc-A-Fella Records for an estimated $1.4 million, giving founders Jay-Z and Damon Dash part ownership of the label, while Def Jam maintained distribution and co-marketing.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-14) That same year, through Def Jam A&R Irv Gotti, Def Jam signed artist DMX.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-15)

**Def Jam Recordings** (also simply known as **Def Jam** or **Def Jam Records**) is an American multinational record label owned by Universal Music Group. It is based in Manhattan, New York City, specializing predominantly in hip-hop, contemporary R&B, soul and pop.
The label has a London-based, UK arm known as **0207 Def Jam** (formerly **Def Jam UK** in the 1990s until the mid-2000s) and is currently operated through Polydor Records.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-:1-2) It has a Johannesburg, South Africa and Lagos, Nigeria-based arm known as Def Jam Africa.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
[edit]
Def Jam was co-founded by Rick Rubin in his dormitory in Weinstein Hall at New York University,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-3) and its first release was a single by his punk-rock group Hose. Russell Simmons joined Rubin shortly after they were introduced to each other, according to one story, by Vincent Gallo.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-4) Another cites DJ Jazzy Jay as their connector.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-5) Rubin has said he met Simmons on the TV show _Graffiti Rock_ and recognized him then as "the face of hip hop": "He was five years older than me, and he was already established in the music business. And I had no experience whatsoever."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-6) The second single released with the Def Jam Recordings logo was T La Rock& Jazzy Jay's "It's Yours". The first releases with Def Jam Recordings catalog numbers were LL Cool J's "I Need a Beat" and the Beastie Boys' "Rock Hard", both in 1984. The singles sold well, eventually leading to a distribution deal with CBS Records through Columbia Records the following year. However, the Hose and T La Rock releases were _not_ part of the deal and are now controlled by different entities.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
This created a short-lived subsidiary label called OBR Records, short for Original Black Recordings, which catered toward R&B artists—the first artist signed to that imprint was [Oran "Juice" Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones "Oran \"Juice\" Jones"), who enjoyed success with his hit single "[The Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rain_(Oran_%22Juice%22_Jones_song) "The Rain (Oran \"Juice\" Jones song)")". A few years later, Russell Simmons and Lyor Cohen started an umbrella label called Rush Associated Labels to handle Def Jam and its numerous spinoff labels. RAL became the home to Nice & Smooth and EPMD after both acts were acquired due to the folding of their former label Sleeping Bag Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-7) Other acts under the RAL umbrella included Redman, Onyx, Flatlinerz, Domino, Warren G and Jayo Felony. Def Jam also signed its first and only thrash metal band, Slayer, in 1986, and the band's third and fourth albums were the only two Def Jam releases to be distributed through Geffen Records via Warner Bros. Records as opposed to Columbia/CBS. As the decade drew to a close, the label signed Public Enemy, whose controversial lyrical content garnered the company both critical acclaim and disdain. Lyor Cohen became president of Def Jam/RAL in 1988, after winning a power struggle with Rubin, who would shortly thereafter leave the company to form Def American Recordings. Rubin would take Slayer and the rights of its Def Jam albums with him to Def American in its initial stages.

### Founding and CBS Records Group era (1983–1994)
In 1991, CBS Records was folded (or rather rebranded) to the music division of Japanese electronic giant Sony, bringing Def Jam and Columbia with it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-9) By 1992, despite recent multiple platinum selling releases from Public Enemy, and EPMD, Def Jam ran into major financial troubles and was faced with folding while at Sony. That year, Kevin Liles was hired as an intern.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-10)

### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
[edit]
In 1994, PolyGram purchased Sony's 50% stake in Def Jam Recordings—subsequently bringing the label into the Island Records fold. Island would share in sales and marketing duties with select radio projects while Def Jam remained independent on all other label functions (A&R, video, promotion and publicity). The label venture went on to receive huge success with a slew of various other multi-platinum releases from Montell Jordan, Public Enemy, LL Cool J, Redman, Method Man and more. RAL/Def Jam also distributed the Violator Records-signed artist Warren G's debut album, _Regulate... G Funk Era_, which went triple platinum and brought much-needed revenue to Def Jam through its joint deal with Violator.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-11)
PolyGram acquired an additional 10% stake in Def Jam, further strengthening its ownership of the label. Shortly thereafter, Rush Associated Labels were renamed to the Def Jam Music Group. The label remained profitable as its veteran star LL Cool J released his successful album _Mr. Smith_ in 1995, a return to the rapper's original credibility following the fallback of his 1993 album, _14 Shots to the Dome_; his last album under the Def Jam/Columbia partnership.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-12) The label later signed Foxy Brown, whose debut album, _Ill Na Na_ (1996) became a platinum seller in 1997.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-13) Def Jam followed up with its then-new R&B act, Case, whose self-titled debut album (also in 1996), including the single, "Touch Me, Tease Me", went gold._[citation needed_]

### PolyGram era (1994–1998)
In June 1997, Def Jam acquired 50% of rapper Jay-Z's Roc-A-Fella Records for an estimated $1.4 million, giving founders Jay-Z and Damon Dash part ownership of the label, while Def Jam maintained distribution and co-marketing.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-14) That same year, through Def Jam A&R Irv Gotti, Def Jam signed artist DMX.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-15)

Home/Denda/Diskoetxeak/Def Jam Recordings
New York hip-hop label founded in 1983 by Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin. It has since gone on to become one of the most well-known hip-hop labels in the world, along the way making stars of the likes of Public Enemy, L.L. Cool J, The Beastie Boys, Redman, and DMX.
Chairman and CEO from 2022: Tunji Balogun.
See also [l=Def Jam Music Group Inc.], [l=Def Jam Recordings Group Inc.], [l=Def Jam Recordings Music Group], [l=Def Jam Recordings Music Group Inc.], [l=Def Jam 2000], [l=Def Jam Germany].
For counterfeit releases, see [l172430].
History:
1984: Label founded; releases several 12″ singles independently. First release was purchased by Streetwise Records and released with a Def Jam logo (and is not considered part of Def Jam today).
1985: Def Jam Recordings began distribution through Columbia/CBS Records.
1988: CBS Records was purchased by the Sony Corporation.
1991: CBS Records became Sony Music Entertainment.
1994: PolyGram purchased 50% of Sony’s Def Jam holdings and switches distribution companies.
1996: PolyGram purchased an additional 10% of the Def Jam holdings, which made it the parent company.
1999: Universal Music Group was formed through the merger of the MCA and PolyGram families of labels and it subsequently purchased the remaining Def Jam holdings that Sony held. All the Def Jam assets were then spun into Island Def Jam Music Group after merging it with Mercury’s pop roster and Island Records.
2004: Universal Music Japan begins using the Def Jam Recordings imprint within its [l=Universal Sigma] label division for domestic Japanese releases (operating independently of the Island Def Jam Music Group).
2013: Barry Weiss stepped down as Chairman/CEO of both Island and Def Jam.
2014: [l=Universal Music] dissolved The [l=Island Def Jam Music Group]. Now re-positioned Def Jam, [l=Island Records] and [l=Motown] separately as all three solo labels.

2017: Universal Music Japan begins using the Def Jam Recordings imprint within its [l=Virgin Music (4)] label division for domestic Japanese releases (operating independently of Def Jam).
2024: Def Jam, Island and [l=Republic Records] join under UMG’s east coast operations as [l=Republic Corps].
Label code: LC 08427 / LC 8427.

## **How DMX and Jay-Z fueled the Def Jam sale**
Better business for whom? Is probably a good place to put it. But I agree with the broader sentiment of if you’re trying to tell the story of hip hop, you’re trying to capture the journey, especially once you get past the early years of hip hop’s founding and what really helped craft the art form to what it is. And this is probably a good place to get into some of the backstory here. Def Jam created what people identify as the modern record label, and its founders had a big influence on what people consider to be hip hop and how people think about hip hop, not just the music, but all of its various extensions. And those two founders, Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin, I think it’s interesting to look at what they were doing before Def Jam and how they got to this spot. How they got to this spot. So, of course, famously, the record label idea comes from Rick Rubin himself. And he’s a student at NYU, and he’s in his dorm room. He was really interested in rock music and producing and making music, but really wanted to lean into a record label and he wanted to create his own imprint. And he really identified with a lot of hip hop. I think one of the things that he said that stuck out to him was a lot of the hip hop at the time was much more focused on taking soul records or taking disco records and then rapping over them. That was definitely a lot of the Sugar Hill record style production. But there wasn’t as much of the true beat making The B-Boys and the style and the aesthetic that was a bit more native to what people think about. When you think about hardcore New York hip hop in that type of way or even things like how a verse leads into a chorus and then you have another verse and then you repeat that chorus again, something that sounds so obvious. It really wasn’t that. And I think that’s one of the things that Ruben really helped craft, especially in those early years.
Zack O’Malley Greenburg [00:06:01]:

## **How DMX and Jay-Z fueled the Def Jam sale**
Yeah, definitely. And it’s such an unlikely pairing, right? I mean, you have Russell Simmons, who was kind of bouncing around the early days of hip hop, helping elevate some of the early superstars like Curtis Blow selling fake weed on the side, or so he says. And, you know, like Rick Rubin, who’s just but I don’t know. Was he a hippie back then, too? Did he have the hair and the beard? I don’t know. But he know this hard rocking college student know really into thrash metal and stuff like of it’s kind kind of a strange mix. But like you say, that’s kind of the magic that created Def Jam. And I think Rick Rubin really did give hip hop a harder edge. And weirdly, I think it came from rock, right? It was that rock, that kind of like metal sensibility that maybe kind of took the flashy shine off a little bit of that sort of early disco rap, like the early kind of stuff that Russell Simmons was pushing and gave it that a bit of an edge. Which is funny because hip hop, of course, originated from the streets in the South Bronx and stuff. But it did have that disco element. So in a way, it was like coming downtown, getting the rock aspect added to it that made it musically sound like a little harder edge. And certainly when you start to see like, Cool J and you know, it sounds definitely different from the very disco inflected kind of early hip hop. Yeah, quite an OD marriage, I think. Not the most harmonious marriage all the time, but I think in the way that sometimes that’s how you get the best creative work. Lenon, McCartney, or if you look at even Jay Z and Nas over the years, I know they didn’t necessarily work together, but like pushing each other know, inspiring each other to create better know simply through their rivalry. And so, yeah, I think that’s kind of what you got in some way from Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons and.
Dan Runcie [00:08:21]:

## **How DMX and Jay-Z fueled the Def Jam sale**
How these two met always sticks out to me. So they met at this party for this TV show in the early 80s called Graffiti Rock. It’s this pilot episode that they were having. And then they meet there and they knew of each other’s work. Ruben was really admiring what Simmons was doing, especially at the time, he had had Rush Productions and he was having several artists on his roster. And he was also wanting and Simmons himself, he was the one that wanted to meet Rick Rubin because he’s like, oh, who’s the guy that made this record? Who’s the guy that did this? And then someone points to Rick Rubin, and of course, Russell Simmons sees him point to this white guy and he’s like, Wait, the white boy. So it’s this pretty common thing that we see, where you see someone, you’re like, oh, this is who it is. But they are able to figure it out. And I think what stuck for Simmons is that, okay, it doesn’t make sense to have these two things separate. Meaning the record label that Rick Rubin is trying to start and the management and the production that Russell Simmons is trying to do. So he wants to bring them together, and then they get things going. And then that’s when, 1984, they officially do start Def Jam recordings. And deaf, of course, as Rick Rubin says it, we’ll get to this later. But Def being word to describe, okay, this is something that’s cool. This is hip, this is what’s up. And then, Jsm, more so the aspect of making the music and enjoying it. But it’s funny because if you ask Russell Simmons, he’ll say that Rick Rubin was more of the deaf and that he was more of the Jam. So they’ve always kind of had an interesting split in terms of how they saw things. And I think, as you alluded to, we’ll get into this, but how some of that led to some of the challenges that they have. But they were able to at least get the first few records off the ground, get things moving, and things really start to change for them when they get the first big deal that they get for the record label is a deal with CBS. At the time, through Columbia, they were able to get a six figure production and distribution deal for Def Jam.

## **How DMX and Jay-Z fueled the Def Jam sale**
And that then gives them the ability to then pick four acts per year. I saw some reports that said it was around 600,000. I’m not sure how exact that is, but I do know that it was a six figure deal. And this is a landmark because this is the first time that a major record label at the time had done a deal with hip hop music in this type of way.
Zack O’Malley Greenburg [00:10:57]:
Yeah, and it’s a landmark deal for sure. But don’t forget, Russell Simmons was making moves like this, not just on the musical side. In that period of time in the mid 80s, you think of the Adidas deal that he got Run DMC bringing the Adidas executives to the garden in a skybox. And of course, Run DMC goes out, they say, Everybody put your Adidas in the air. They put their Adidas in the air, 20,000 screaming fans, and then Run DMC plays my Adidas. And that’s how Russell Simmons convinced these executives to give Run DMC a million dollar sneaker deal. So it’s kind of interesting. This is all happening around the same time, right? The music and the know with Def Jam, with RunDMC, et cetera.
Dan Runcie [00:11:46]:

**Def Jam Recordings** (also simply known as **Def Jam** or **Def Jam Records**) is an American multinational record label owned by Universal Music Group. It is based in Manhattan, New York City, specializing predominantly in hip-hop, contemporary R&B, soul and pop.
The label has a London-based, UK arm known as **0207 Def Jam** (formerly **Def Jam UK** in the 1990s until the mid-2000s) and is currently operated through Polydor Records.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam_Recordings#cite_note-:1-2) It has a Johannesburg, South Africa and Lagos, Nigeria-based arm known as Def Jam Africa.
